name: COPPA: Children Under 13
title: COPPA: Children Under 13
answer: COPPA requires companies that run websites and apps to get confirmed permission from a parent before collecting personal information from a child under 13. Schools can consent on behalf of parents only when the information is used for a purpose the school has authorized for education and for no other commercial purpose. This matters for AI because many general chat tools set a minimum age of 13, some require parental permission under 18, and UNESCO guidance recommends 13 as the minimum age for independent conversations with generative AI.

crumbs.name: Privacy, Safety, and the Human Review Rule

sections.body: COPPA is a privacy rule for children under 13. It puts the first duty on companies that run websites and apps, which must get a parent's confirmed permission before collecting a child's personal information. In schools, the Federal Trade Commission allows a shortcut: a school can give that permission for parents, but only for a purpose the school has authorized for education and not for any other commercial reason. The FTC also recommends that the school or district make that decision rather than individual teachers, and that parents be told which services the school has approved. For AI, the practical issue is age, because many general chat tools require users to be at least 13 and some require parental permission for anyone under 18.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In the early grades, most AI use belongs with the teacher rather than the child, so the child is not independently using a tool that collects personal information. For older students, the school should follow the age rules listed for each named product, including the common minimum age of 13 and any parental permission required under 18. UNESCO guidance recommends 13 as the minimum age for independent conversations with generative AI. When a school approves a service for a purpose the school has authorized for education, the school or district can consent on behalf of parents, but it must not allow the information to be used for any other commercial purpose. The school or district should make the approval decision, not individual teachers, and parents should be told which services have been approved.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: This idea rests on regulatory and enforcement sources rather than research, and the book does not attach a research evidence label to it. It cites the Federal Trade Commission, 2020 for the school consent shortcut. It cites the Federal Trade Commission, 2023 for an action against Edmodo, which the FTC said had about 600,000 users under 13 in 2020 alone, for gathering children's information without proper consent, using it for advertising, and shifting its COPPA duties onto schools and teachers. It cites the Federal Register, 2025 for the 2025 update, which requires full compliance by April 22, 2026, separate parental consent before a child's information is shared with third parties such as advertisers, and keeping children's data only as long as it is reasonably needed. It cites Miao & Holmes, 2023 for UNESCO guidance recommending 13 as the minimum age for independent conversations with generative AI.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: Final responsibility for complying rests with the company, not the school, but a school still has reason to check because its students are exposed when a company gets it wrong. The limit on commercial use is enforced, and the FTC action against Edmodo shows the risk of pushing COPPA duties onto schools and teachers. The FTC thought about making separate rules for education technology but decided against it, pointing to possible changes in FERPA. A separate bill often called COPPA 2.0 would cover teens up to 16, but it had not become law when the book was written. Decisions about consent and approved services stay with the school or district, not individual teachers, and parents should be told which services the school has approved; this is a description of practice, not legal advice.
